*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Something feels off with this chorus of “India’s internet is great and super cheap” … the data shows that Indian market is absolutely dominated by mobile. When they say it’s cheap and well connected factually this only applies to mobile usage. 

This makes sense because a tower connects thousands of subs instantly after construction and running fiber is a building by building or resident by resident job. This is also why “fixed wireless” has started growing fast. Follow the incentives. It’s the cheapest and shortest route to revenue. 

Due to this, India is amongst the highest mobile bandwidth usage populations on the planet. 30-40GB/month. (20-50% above US/UK usage) However, home Fiber lines in India pull closer to 300GB/month. 10x gap

For context, that gap in the US and UK is 20-30x. It’s pretty ubiquitous that if you have access to a lot of more bandwidth you will use it. 

Bandwidth abundance does not favor mobile devices. 

I’d argue that it’s not very hard to believe that these paltry sub 5% fixed customer penetration numbers would be much higher if a cost effective alternative existed.

Is that alternative existed it wouldn’t be crazy to expect to see the fixed customer numbers jump from 6% to maybe 10%, 15% or 20%. 100M-200M customers. 

And if the rest of the world is any precedent that would lead to a dramatic increase in overall bandwidth used. 

However, that would mean that mobile bandwidth usage would likely drop or stagnate with in home mobile usage.

While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Exercise democratic rights responsibly. Keep actions peaceful, follow lawful restrictions and seek remedies through proper forums. An assembly without permission risks becoming an unlawful gathering under existing criminal laws.

Concerns about electoral rolls or any public issue must rest on verified facts and formal processes. Blocking roads or gathering without sanction crosses into illegality. The Constitution permits protest only within reasonable limits of public order.

WHEN THE INTERNET IS SHUT DOWN, THE RIGHT TO COMMUNICATE DOESN’T SIMPLY DISAPPEAR

The BitChat episode raises a much bigger question than one app.

BitChat is designed to allow nearby phones to communicate through Bluetooth mesh, without depending on mobile internet, SIM cards or a central messaging server. Its popularity reportedly surged in India during protests where internet connectivity was restricted.

On 3 October 2026, Apple removed BitChat from the Indian App Store following a government direction under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act. The Internet Freedom Foundation has questioned the legality and proportionality of blocking an entire communications application, particularly when the specific allegedly unlawful content has not been publicly identified.

The democratic principle is simple:

Internet shutdown ≠ shutdown of citizenship.

A democracy must be able to distinguish between:
• unlawful conduct and lawful communication;
• specific harmful content and an entire communications tool;
• legitimate security concerns and disproportionate restrictions;
• regulation and suppression of the ability of citizens to communicate.

The answer to concerns about misuse should be due process, transparency and targeted action—not automatically making ordinary citizens unable to communicate with one another.

The government should publicly disclose the legal basis and specific grounds for the blocking order, and affected developers should have meaningful access to legal remedies.

Technology will keep evolving. Democratic safeguards must evolve with it.

Protect communication. Protect due process. Protect the constitutional space for peaceful citizenship.

#India: The internet shutdown targeting protesters, which affected businesses and gig workers, was geographically the largest curb in Delhi since the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, writes @AroonDeep

Read full article: https://t.co/4bb1M6RjuK via @the_hindu

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Delhi ahead of the 10 October protest. The order remains unpublished, and the police communication conveying it is marked "Top Secret".

9 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the internet shutdown imposed in parts of Delhi ahead of the protest called for tomorrow, 10 October 2026, at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. A communication dated 9 October 2026 from the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Special Cell (HQ), Delhi to the nodal officers of Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Jio and MTNL, shared by the news agency ANI, records that the Union Home Secretary has authorised, on the request of the Delhi Police, the suspension of "mobile internet services (all technologies)" within a radius of four kilometres of the Janpath-Kartavya Path crossing, from 10 pm on 9 October to 10 pm on 10 October 2026. It refers to order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and is marked "Top Secret" at the top and bottom of the page.

As per a media report by Live Law, the Solicitor General informed the Supreme Court today that the shutdown is confined to "certain sensitive pockets" and will be reviewed on the basis of security inputs. The communication describes a circle of about 50 square kilometres across the centre of the capital, which takes in Jantar Mantar, Connaught Place, India Gate, Parliament, the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court, New Delhi Railway Station and hospitals including Ram Manohar Lohia and Lady Hardinge. This is about seven times the area of the suspension ordered around Jantar Mantar on 2 October, and it runs for twice as long.

Delhi Police has refused permission for the protest, and prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force in New Delhi district. Delhi Police asked for the gates of 57 metro stations to be closed from 9 pm today, and the Railways cancelled trains due at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin between 4 am and 2 pm tomorrow. Hearing a challenge to these measures today, the Supreme Court directed that there be no complete prohibition on metro and train services and asked the authorities to keep in mind the principle of proportionality. As reported, that order did not examine the internet shutdown. We call for the order to be withdrawn, and for mobile internet to remain available across Delhi tomorrow.

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public knows the area and hours of this shutdown from a police communication marked "Top Secret" that was shared by ANI, and not from the government. That communication records no reasons, and the order of the Union Home Secretary to which it refers has not been made public. This is now a pattern and the order for the shutdown of 2 October around Jantar Mantar became public four days later, when the Hindu obtained a copy.

This secrecy is contrary to the law declared by the Supreme Court. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Court held that "an order, particularly one that affects lives, liberty and property of people, must be made available". It directed the authorities to "publish all orders in force and any future orders" suspending telecom services, including the internet, "to enable the affected persons to challenge it before the High Court or appropriate forum". A democracy "sworn to transparency and accountability", the Court said, "necessarily mandates the production of orders as it is the right of an individual to know". The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, framed under Section 20 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, now provide that every suspension order "shall be published", must state its reasons, and must be limited to a clearly defined geographical area and a specified duration. No order may be made unless the authority has considered that its objectives cannot be achieved by any other reasonable means.

The communication shared by ANI invokes Rule 3 of these Rules, the same Rule that requires the order to be published. It is nevertheless marked "Top Secret", the highest security classification used by the Government of India. In January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued orders bearing the same number to suspend the internet at Singhu, Ghazipur and Tikri during the farmers' protest, and those orders remain available on the Ministry's own website. An order cannot be published and kept "Top Secret" at the same time.

The government has placed no evidence before the public that a shutdown makes a protest safer. The available research is to the contrary as a 2019 study of shutdowns and protest in India by Jan Rydzak, then at Stanford's Global Digital Policy Incubator, found shutdowns "much more strongly associated with increases in violent collective action than with non-violent mobilization". The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights reported in 2022 that many shutdowns justified on grounds of public safety or national security "were followed by spikes in violence" (A/HRC/50/55). In December 2021, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology recorded that neither the Department of Telecommunications nor the Ministry of Home Affairs had studied the impact of shutdowns.

A shutdown also prevents people from documenting and reporting what happens at a protest. The same UN report found that, “the inability to access tools to document and rapidly report abuses seems to contribute to further violence”. Without mobile internet, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A protester cannot upload a video as events unfold, and a person who is injured or detained cannot send a location to family or a lawyer. On 20 July 2026, mobile internet in Central Delhi was switched off amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters. In Manipur in 2023, video of an assault on two women on 4 May reached the public only on 19 July, while a shutdown imposed on 3 May was still in force. This is the impact an internet shutdown has which rather than preventing violence prevents the documentation of illegality.

Our demands:

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Delhi Police to:
1) Withdraw order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and keep mobile internet services running across Delhi on 10 October 2026.
2) Publish that order, and every other suspension order issued in connection with the protest, forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.
3) Withdraw the "Top Secret" marking, and stop classifying suspension orders and the communications that convey them to telecom operators.
4) Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and publish its final order, as the Supreme Court required on 23 February 2024.
5) Ensure that journalists and members of the public can record and report from the protest sites without obstruction.

The ridiculous arguments by Ambani’s army of Internet shills make no sense

On the one hand, they say Starlink couldn’t possibly compete with the amazing low prices offered by Ambani’s de facto monopoly in India and then, in the same breath, they essentially claim that Starlink would be too strong of a competitor! This is absurd hypocrisy and hyperbole. 

The reality is that competition would greatly benefit the average citizen in India by giving them more choices, as it always does. Ambani’s profits will be lower, but he is not going out of business. And, obviously, if Starlink is too expensive in India, no one will buy it, so SpaceX will need to make pricing affordable.

quotedTweet.text:
Something feels off with this chorus of “India’s internet is great and super cheap” … the data shows that Indian market is absolutely dominated by mobile. When they say it’s cheap and well connected factually this only applies to mobile usage. 

This makes sense because a tower connects thousands of subs instantly after construction and running fiber is a building by building or resident by resident job. This is also why “fixed wireless” has started growing fast. Follow the incentives. It’s the cheapest and shortest route to revenue. 

Due to this, India is amongst the highest mobile bandwidth usage populations on the planet. 30-40GB/month. (20-50% above US/UK usage) However, home Fiber lines in India pull closer to 300GB/month. 10x gap

For context, that gap in the US and UK is 20-30x. It’s pretty ubiquitous that if you have access to a lot of more bandwidth you will use it. 

Bandwidth abundance does not favor mobile devices. 

I’d argue that it’s not very hard to believe that these paltry sub 5% fixed customer penetration numbers would be much higher if a cost effective alternative existed.

Is that alternative existed it wouldn’t be crazy to expect to see the fixed customer numbers jump from 6% to maybe 10%, 15% or 20%. 100M-200M customers. 

And if the rest of the world is any precedent that would lead to a dramatic increase in overall bandwidth used. 

However, that would mean that mobile bandwidth usage would likely drop or stagnate with in home mobile usage.

Lauren Dreyer, SpaceX's Vice President of Starlink Business Operations, spoke at India Mobile Congress in New Delhi today. She thanked the Government of India and the Department of Telecommunications for the chance to share Starlink's vision. Her message: "We stand ready to serve India, as soon as India is ready!"

Starlink says it has spent the past five years working with Indian regulators, industry and operators. The goal was to adapt its operations to serve India, and to meet Indian security needs. It says it can help reach places where the last mile is still the hardest mile, working alongside India's operators, government and industry. It also says it can help accelerate efforts to connect India 100%.

The ground work is done. Starlink has built 20 gateway sites in India, with hundreds of antennas. It has security controls tailored to Indian requirements. Indian user data will stay within the country.

The remaining step is government authorisation. Under the DoT's current authorisation terms, satellite communication operators must also pay an annual licence fee of 8% of AGR.

Reaction is split. Some investors see India as a huge market for Starlink. Some critics want it banned, citing security fears.

The revised outlook is driven by CARE Edge Ratings' expectation of sustained operational scale and likely improvement in profitability for SAIL in the short-to-medium term. This optimism stems from significant measures implemented by the company over the past two fiscals.

- 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁: Profit before interest, lease, depreciation & tax (PBILDT) per tonne has shown a significant increase, rising from ₹6,998 in Q1FY26 to ₹9,974 in Q1FY27, and is expected to remain healthy. This improvement is attributed to cost-efficiency measures, the expected commencement of the Tasra coking coal mine, and increased monetization of surplus iron ore.
- '𝗠𝗮𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗻𝗮' 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘁𝘂𝘀 & 𝗚𝗼𝗹 𝗦𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁: SAIL's ratings continue to benefit from its 'Maharatna' status & strong support from the Government of India (GoI), which holds a 65% stake. This provides financial & operational flexibility and access to funding at competitive rates.
- 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁 𝗣𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: As one of India's largest integrated steel manufacturers, SAIL holds a strong market position & is a critical supplier for government projects, Indian Railways, and defense.

- 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗛𝗲𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗵: Overall gearing improved to 0.63x as of March 31, 2026, from 0.77x a year prior, due to strong cash flow from operations leading to a decline in total debt to ₹35,788 crore from ₹41,740 crore.

This is partially mitigated through a shared procurement mechanism & diverse supplier portfolio. The Tasra coal mine's commencement is expected to improve supply diversification.
- 𝗖𝘆𝗰𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘆: The steel industry is inherently cyclical and capital-intensive.
- 𝗖𝗮𝗽𝗲𝘅 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻𝘀: SAIL plans a significant capacity expansion to ~35 MTPA by FY31-FY32, with an estimated investment of ₹1-1.20 lakh crore, expected to be funded 50:50 by debt & equity. quotedTweet.text:
Something feels off with this chorus of “India’s internet is great and super cheap” … the data shows that Indian market is absolutely dominated by mobile. When they say it’s cheap and well connected factually this only applies to mobile usage. 

This makes sense because a tower connects thousands of subs instantly after construction and running fiber is a building by building or resident by resident job. This is also why “fixed wireless” has started growing fast. Follow the incentives. It’s the cheapest and shortest route to revenue. 

Due to this, India is amongst the highest mobile bandwidth usage populations on the planet. 30-40GB/month. (20-50% above US/UK usage) However, home Fiber lines in India pull closer to 300GB/month. 10x gap

For context, that gap in the US and UK is 20-30x. It’s pretty ubiquitous that if you have access to a lot of more bandwidth you will use it. 

Bandwidth abundance does not favor mobile devices. 

I’d argue that it’s not very hard to believe that these paltry sub 5% fixed customer penetration numbers would be much higher if a cost effective alternative existed.

Is that alternative existed it wouldn’t be crazy to expect to see the fixed customer numbers jump from 6% to maybe 10%, 15% or 20%. 100M-200M customers. 

And if the rest of the world is any precedent that would lead to a dramatic increase in overall bandwidth used. 

However, that would mean that mobile bandwidth usage would likely drop or stagnate with in home mobile usage.

🇮🇳 | Elon Musk, India Doesn’t Fear Starlink — But Foreign Control is a No-go

“A nation’s sovereignty is not negotiable.” — Atal Bihari Vajpayee

Elon Musk says delaying Starlink is a “crime against the people of India.”

No, Elon.

Nobody in India is against a village getting internet.

India is against one man holding the Kill-switch.

🛰️ We have seen this movie before

🇺🇦 Ukraine was operating tens of thousands of Starlink terminals during the war.

Then came Crimea.

Musk refused to extend Starlink coverage there.

Ukrainian sea drones reportedly lost connectivity during an operation.

Think about that for a moment.

A sovereign country’s military capability was affected by the decision of a private businessman thousands of kilometres away.

That is precisely the kind of strategic dependency India has every reason to examine carefully.

⚠️ Then there is Manipur

In December 2024, Indian security forces reportedly recovered a Starlink terminal alongside weapons from a militant cache in Manipur.

Starlink said its network was not active over India.

Fine.

But that raises another question:

How are Starlink terminals reaching conflict zones and the hands of actors who should never have access to them?

🇮🇳 India isn't blocking Starlink

Let's get this straight.

Starlink isn't simply being “banned” by some anti-technology bureaucracy.

The company has already secured key regulatory approvals.

What remains involves spectrum allocation and security requirements.

That's not an oligarchic conspiracy.

That's a sovereign government asking a foreign satellite operator some very basic questions before allowing its network to operate across Indian territory.

🔐 Connectivity is infrastructure

A satellite network isn't just another consumer app.

It can become part of:

📡 Communications
🛰️ Critical infrastructure
🛡️ National security
🚨 Emergency response
⚔️ Military operations

And when the network is controlled by a private company headquartered outside India, questions about data, lawful access, network control, security auditing and continuity during a crisis aren't optional.

They're the whole point.

🎯 Strategic Lens

So yes, Elon.
Bring Starlink to India's villages.
Bring it to the mountains.
Bring it to the islands.
Bring connectivity to every Indian who needs it.
But do it on India's terms.

🇮🇳 Data stays under Indian jurisdiction.
🔐 Security audits happen under Indian rules.
⚖️ Indian law applies on Indian soil.
🛰️ And no switch in Texas decides what works over India during a national crisis.

That's not anti-progress.
That's sovereignty.

Something feels off with this chorus of “India’s internet is great and super cheap” … the data shows that Indian market is absolutely dominated by mobile. When they say it’s cheap and well connected factually this only applies to mobile usage. 

This makes sense because a tower connects thousands of subs instantly after construction and running fiber is a building by building or resident by resident job. This is also why “fixed wireless” has started growing fast. Follow the incentives. It’s the cheapest and shortest route to revenue. 

Due to this, India is amongst the highest mobile bandwidth usage populations on the planet. 30-40GB/month. (20-50% above US/UK usage) However, home Fiber lines in India pull closer to 300GB/month. 10x gap

For context, that gap in the US and UK is 20-30x. It’s pretty ubiquitous that if you have access to a lot of more bandwidth you will use it. 

Bandwidth abundance does not favor mobile devices. 

I’d argue that it’s not very hard to believe that these paltry sub 5% fixed customer penetration numbers would be much higher if a cost effective alternative existed.

Is that alternative existed it wouldn’t be crazy to expect to see the fixed customer numbers jump from 6% to maybe 10%, 15% or 20%. 100M-200M customers. 

And if the rest of the world is any precedent that would lead to a dramatic increase in overall bandwidth used. 

However, that would mean that mobile bandwidth usage would likely drop or stagnate with in home mobile usage.

text:
DO NOT DO BUSINESS IN INDIA!

What exists is an Indian antitrust case in which the maximum penalty could be calculated on Apple’s global revenue, and Apple is fighting that formula in court.
India’s Competition Commission (CCI) has been investigating Apple’s App Store since 2021. Developers and groups including Match (Tinder), PhonePe and Paytm accused Apple of abusing a dominant position by forcing apps to use Apple’s in-app payment system and charging a commission of up to 30%. Apple denies the allegations. A final penalty order had still not been issued as of the latest reporting in September 2026; the Delhi High Court had barred the CCI from issuing one before 15 July 2026 while Apple’s challenge was pending.
The global-revenue issue comes from a 2023 amendment to the Competition Act and the CCI’s 2024 penalty guidelines. Those rules let the regulator fine a company up to 10% of its average global turnover from all products and services over the previous three financial years, not only India revenue or App Store revenue. Apple told the Delhi High Court that, applied to FY2022–FY2024, that cap would be about $38 billion. Its India revenue is far smaller — about $8.9 billion in FY25, against roughly $416 billion worldwide.
The CCI’s stated reason is deterrence. It argues that a fine based only on India sales would be too small to change the behavior of a global digital company, and that the global-turnover rule matches practice used in the EU. Apple calls the rule arbitrary, disproportionate and unconstitutional when the alleged conduct is limited to India, and has asked the court to strike it down. In May 2026 the CCI also shifted, at least for the investigation, to seeking Apple’s India-specific financials rather than global figures.

मस्क अंबानी को प्रधानमंत्री लिख रहे हैं। भारत की सरकारी फैक्ट चेकर PIB खंडन भी नहीं कर रही है। पूरी भारत सरकार मस्क के आगे चुप है। मंत्री चुप हैं। मस्क अंबानी को नहीं, प्रधानमंत्री मोदी को चैलेंज कर रहे हैं। उनका यह पोस्ट कॉरपोरेट वॉर का इशारा नहीं करता है बल्कि प्रधानमंत्री पद और दफ्तर की गरिमा की ऐसी तैसी कर रहा है। प्रधानमंत्री मोदी भी चुप हैं। यहाँ विपक्ष ज्ञानेश कुमार चोर है का नारा लगाने के लिए जंतर-मंतर जाना चाहता है तो उसे रोक दिया जाता है। जेन ज़ी को दिल्ली आने से रोक दिया जाता है। सारी ताकत विपक्ष पर दिखा रहे हैं, दो लाइन किसी मंत्री से लिखा नहीं जा रहा है कि मस्क जी हम जिस मंत्रिमंडल के मेंबर हैं, उसके प्रधानमंत्री तो नरेंद्र मोदी हैं। आप भूल सुधार कर लीजिए।प्रधानमंत्री पद की गरिमा को मुद्दा बनाने वाली बीजेपी के राष्ट्रीय अध्यक्ष को ही ट्वीट कर देना चाहिए कि प्रधानमंत्री नरेंद्र मोदी हैं, अंबानी नहीं। गोदी मीडिया के ऐंकरों को चिल्लाना चाहिए कि मस्क ग़लती सुधार लो, वरना इस दीवाली फुलझड़ियों को छोड़ टेस्ला के ख़िलाफ अभियान चलाने लगेंगे। सब चुप है। दूसरों को चुप कराने वाले चुप हैं।

जिस मस्क को कभी भारत में जेल जाने से डर लगता था, उस मस्क को क्या हुआ है? क्यों पिनक गए हैं, चिंता की बात होनी चाहिए। सूचना प्रसारण मंत्रालय के मंत्री को एक्स के किसी मैनेजर को बुलाकर पूछना चाहिए कि तुम्हारे मालिक नरेंद्र मोदी को छोड़ अंबानी को कैसे प्रधानमंत्री लिख रहे हैं? यह शपथ कब हुआ है? फोटो दिखाओ? मस्क, अंबानी, अदाणी, सरकार इन सबके बीच जो हो रहा है, उनके बीच सही बात क्या है, किसी को पता तो है नहीं। कौन किसे मैनेज कर रहा है, पर्दे के पीछे के पर्दे के पीछे कौन-कौन है, यह जान लेने से क्या बदल जाता है। मगर प्रधानमंंत्री अंबानी हैं, ये कब बदल गया? राहुल गांधी तो वोट चोरी को प्रधानमंत्री, गृहमंत्री और ज्ञानेश कुमार के प्रोजेक्ट तक ही देख पा रहे हैं, इसके ऊपर का भी मामला है क्या? 

वैसे इस प्लेटफार्म के लिए मस्क आपका शुक्रिया। ठीक है सरकार के कहने पर आप भी पोस्ट हटा देते हैं लेकिन आदमी अपनी बात तो लिख पा रहा है। अगर एक्स करोल बाग के किसी टाइकून का प्लेटफार्म होता तो हम लोगों के प्लेटफार्म के आगे बैरिकेड लगवा देता और डिलीट कर देता। इसलिए आपके पोस्ट पर इधर के उद्योगपति लोग भी चुप हैं। आसान नहीं है आपकी तरह लब-लब कुछ भी बोल देना। इधर सारा आंत्रोपन्योरशिप सरकार से लाइसेंस, ठेका, ज़मीन वाले प्रोजेक्ट लेने में लगा रहता है। ज़िलाधिकारी से लेकर सचिव के चक्कर काटने में लगा रहता है। एक प्रोडक्ट ढंग का नहीं बनता। अपने प्रोडेक्ट को ग्लोबल लेवल पर पहुंचाने के बजाए 24 घंटा इसी में लगे रहते हैं कि सरकार से क्या मिल सकता है। आपको भी वही झेलना पड़ेगा। आप भारत आओ, दीवाली का टाइम है, गिफ्ट-विफ्ट लेकर आओ, बात समझो, आप देखना यही मंत्री लोग आपके साथ कैसे फोटो खिंचाते हैं। आओ तो सही, पूरी सरकार बिछी मिलेगी। मुस्कुरा दोगे पीएम साहब को देख कर तो गोदी मीडिया हेडलाइन बना देगा। अपनी वैल्यू समझो आप। कॉकरोच दिल्ली आ गए हैं और आप उधर से ही पोस्ट फायर किए जा रहे हो। COME.

इसीलिए मस्क जी, भारत के प्रधानमंत्री का नाम नरेंद्र मोदी है। अंबानी नहीं है। भारत में आपकी जीवनी हिन्दी में भी छप चुकी है। आपकी माँ मेय मस्क जी की किताब जब औरत सोचती है, राजकमल प्रकाशन से छप चुकी है।आप एक मामूली पॉलिसी निर्णय को लेकर पिनके हुए हैं, यहां तो करोड़ों लोगों के वोट काट दिए गए हैं। वोट का अधिकार छीन लिया गया है। बात को समझो आप। सोशल मीडिया की तरह वोटर को ब्लॉक कर दिया जाता है। नेता प्रतिपक्ष को धक्का दिया जाता है। स्टार लिंक लेकर आ भी गए होते तो क्या हो जाता, आपका भी आज सीपी और चार किलोमीटर के दायरे में बंद रहता। अच्छा हुआ है आप नहीं आए। वैसे अगर स्टार लिंक का कोई पर्सनल लिंक है तो व्हाट्स एप पर भेज देना। आज जंतर-मंतर से वीडियो अपलिंक करना है। बच्चों को प्यार देना। प्रधानमंत्री नरेंद्र मोदी की तरफ से भी। हम लोग डर जाते हैं मगर प्यार ज़रूर करते हैं। ख़ुश रहिए।

The Manipur High Court has ordered the immediate removal of the viral video showing the killing of Meitei civilian Mayanglambam Rishikanta Singh.

The video relates to the 21 Jan killing in Churachandpur district. MeitY had already issued blocking orders under Section 69A of the IT Act.

text:
Downloading Child Pornography is an Offence?

➡️ According to IT Act, 2000 - Downloading sexually explicit material pertaining to #children is an #offence.

➡️ Also, The National Crime Records Bureau, Ministry of Home Affairs, and the American National Center for Missing & Exploited Children prosecute those who upload child sexual abuse materials (#CSAM).

➡️ The #POCSO Act punishes storage or possession of child pornographic material only if it is done with intent to share, transmit, display, distribute, or for commercial purpose.

#UPSC Aspirants must understand #ITAct, 2000 fully to do justice to questions from this domain.

Read this post to know everything about IT ACT, 2000 👇

1️⃣ What is IT Act?
▪️ The Information Technology Act, 2000 (IT Act) is the primary law in India governing Information Technology (IT) and its applications. It was enacted to:
Facilitate electronic #commerce: Provide legal recognition for electronic transactions and digital signatures.
▪️ Combat cybercrime: Define and penalise various cyber offences like #hacking, data #theft, and online fraud.
▪️ Promote electronic governance: Enable government agencies to deliver services electronically.

2️⃣ Why is IT act required?
▪️ With the increasing reliance on technology in everyday life, a legal framework was needed to address issues like #online fraud, security threats, and #data privacy.

3️⃣ Ministries involved
▪️ Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (#MeitY): Responsible for formulating and implementing IT policies, including the IT Act.
▪️ Ministry of Home Affairs (#MHA): Primarily involved in cybercrime investigation and enforcement.
▪️ Ministry of Law and Justice: Involved in drafting and reviewing amendments to the IT Act.

4️⃣ Important Amendments:
▪️ IT Amendment Act, 2002: Introduced sections dealing with cyber terrorism and obscenity in electronic form.

▪️ IT Amendment Act, 2008: Strengthened cybercrime provisions, introduced data protection obligations, and established the Cyber Appellate Tribunal.
- Strengthened cybercrime provisions: Added new offences like identity theft, data theft, and online fraud. Increased penalties for existing offences.
- Data protection obligations: Introduced the requirement for companies to implement reasonable security practices to protect personal data. This was a first step towards a comprehensive data protection framework, which is still under development.
- Established the Cyber Appellate #Tribunal: Created a dedicated tribunal for handling appeals against orders passed by adjudicating officers under the IT Act.

▪️ IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021:
- These rules, notified under the IT Act, impose various obligations on social media platforms and other online intermediaries, including takedown requests, content moderation, and user verification.
- The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and #DigitalMedia #Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, released in 2021, regulates social media, digital media, and #OTT platforms.
- IT Rules (2021) mandate social media platforms to exercise greater diligence with respect to the content on their platforms.
- The intermediary shall prominently publish on its website, mobile based application or both, as the case may be, the rules and regulations, privacy policy and user agreement for access or usage of its computer resource by any person
- The intermediary shall, as soon as possible, but not later than seventy two hours of the receipt of an order, provide information under its control or possession, or assistance to the Government agency which is lawfully authorised for investigative or protective or cyber security activities, for the purposes of verification of identity, or for the prevention, detection, investigation, or prosecution, of offences under any law for the time being in force, or for cyber security incidents
- The intermediary shall report cyber security incidents and share related information with the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team in accordance with the policies and procedures
- The intermediary shall, within twenty-four hours from the receipt of a complaint made by an individual or any person on his behalf under this sub-rule, in relation to any content which is prima facie in the nature of any material which exposes the private area of such individual, shows such individual in full or partial nudity or shows or depicts such individual in any sexual act or conduct, or is in the nature of impersonation in an electronic form, including artificially morphed images of such individual, take all reasonable and practicable measures to remove or disable access to such content which is hosted, stored, published or transmitted by it
- Appoint a Chief Compliance Officer who shall be responsible for ensuring compliance with the Act and rules
- Appoint a nodal contact person for 24x7 coordination with law enforcement agencies and officers to ensure #compliance to their orders or requisitions made in accordance with the provisions of law or #rules
- Publish periodic compliance report every month mentioning the details of complaints received and action taken thereon
- OTT platforms must adhere to the following rules:
🚩Content classification
🚩Age ratings
🚩Self-regulation
🚩Content removal and compliance officers
🚩Grievance redressal mechanisms
🚩The government has the authority to block content in exceptional cases.

▪️ IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2023:
- Introduced specific regulations for online games, including mandatory registration with self-regulatory bodies and restrictions on harmful content.
- They should not share false information about the Indian government, as confirmed by a fact-checking unit.
- An online intermediary – including social media platforms like #Facebook, #YouTube and #Twitter and internet service providers like #Airtel, #Jio and #Vodafone #Idea – should make “reasonable efforts” to not host content related to the Central Government that is “identified as #fake or #misleading” by a “fact check unit” that may be notified by the IT Ministry.

Self-Regulatory Bodies:
- Platforms providing online gaming will have to register with a Self-Regulatory Body (SRB) that will determine whether or not the game is "permissible."
- The platform should ensure that online games do not involve any gambling or betting elements. They should also comply with legal requirements, standards, and safety precautions such as #parentalcontrols.

Losing Safe Harbour:
- If any piece of information is marked as fake by the upcoming fact check unit, intermediaries will be required to take it down, failing which they would risk losing their safe harbour, which protects them from litigation against third-party content.
- Social media sites will have to take down such posts, and internet service providers will have to block URLs of such content

text:
I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly condemns the restriction of its Instagram post discussing the censorship faced by digital fact-checking organisation Alt News, as well as the subsequent takedown of an Instagram Story in which https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 shared Scroll’s report on the matter.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 on 17th September 2026 had published a post highlighting the takedowns faced by Alt News in relation to its reporting on the Chauhaan film teaser. Alt News on 19th August 2026 had published a report on the content takedown they had faced, which was as follows. An Instagram post by Alt News based on the analysis of the teaser of the movie ‘Chauhaan’ was restricted by Instagram. A subsequent version was also removed, while a third version, after references to Hizbul Mujahideen militant “Burhan Wani” were removed, was allowed to remain online. Alt News also stated that search results for “Burhan Wani” on Instagram yielded no results and instead showed a message that said “these search terms may be associated with socially sensitive content”.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has been actively monitoring content takedowns through its Free Speech Tracker and had written extensively about the restrictions faced by Alt News and made a social media post discussing these particular instances to highlight the growing use of opaque content moderation systems on platforms and the chilling effect such systems can have on journalism and public-interest speech. The post specifically noted that such censorship can operate even without a formal government order, and that journalists may begin self-censoring if they believe that certain subjects, words or images could trigger restrictions.

Instagram subsequently restricted https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s posts in India. The notification stated that the content was restricted through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements.” The matter became even more concerning when Scroll reported on the restrictions faced by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 and Alt News in a post on Instagram. When https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 shared Scroll’s report on the matter through an Instagram Story on its public handle, the Story was also taken down by Instagram through the use of automated systems.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 is deeply concerned about the increasing reliance on automated systems for implementing content restrictions and legal compliance requirements. The lack of clarity around this notification further adds to the concern. Since the content has been taken down by automated systems it is unclear whether the restriction stems from a specific legal request or order issued to Meta, or whether Meta has restricted the content suo motu through its automated systems as part of its compliance with the due diligence requirements under the Information Technology Rules, 2021. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has not been provided with sufficient information to determine the source of the restriction, the specific legal basis for it, or the process through which the decision can be challenged.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 emphasises that journalists and news outlets are facing systemic suppression due to over-automated content moderation systems that lack context for investigative reporting, public interest documentation, and critical commentary. By conflating legitimate reporting on sensitive or controversial issues with violations of Community Standards or legal requirements through automated moderation, Meta effectively silences public-interest journalism without human oversight. This opaque suppression undermines press freedom, as well as the public’s right to reliable information, and leaves users without timely recourse to contest improper takedowns.

This situation is exacerbated by the fact that the official Grievance Officer intake form for reporting does not provide a method to report the takedown of content, either for violations of Meta Community Standards, Terms of Service, or through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements”. The response from the Meta AI support assistant instead asks users to physically send an email to the resident Grievance Officer, creating an entirely separate standard for reporting content takedown as opposed to other grievances. As per the Meta platforms the email available on the website can only be used to enquire about the grievance redressal mechanism and not to file a Grievance Office report. This not only creates excessive additional friction for users, but in the case of news reporting, effectively silences journalists and curbs the spread of information for significant periods of time. This also creates a structural barrier to access further remedies such as approaching the Grievance Appellate Committee, which mandatorily requires a Grievance Officer report to be filed prior to filing an appeal.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon Meta to restore https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s post with immediate effect and provide a clear explanation of the legal basis for the takedown. Meta must also ensure meaningful human oversight for restrictions and provide users with an effective and timely mechanism to challenge erroneous takedown especially if done by automated systems. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 further calls upon the Government to provide greater transparency about the legal and policy basis for content restrictions and to clarify whether restrictions were imposed pursuant to government or law-enforcement requests or through Meta’s own systems. The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible and timely avenues to contest takedowns.

What Just Happened?

The Supreme Court, through a bench led by CJI Sanjiv Khanna and Justice Sanjay Kumar, has allowed the Advocate Commissioner to submit the survey report on the Sambhal Mosque to the trial court, but in a sealed cover. This is a big deal because:

1. No Stay Order: The SC didn't put a stay on the trial court's order to survey the mosque. This means the process isn't halted; it's just moving forward under wraps.

2. Masjid Committee's Next Move: The court has directed the Masjid Committee to approach the High Court, indicating that the legal battle is far from over. This gives the committee a chance to contest the survey's implications at a higher judicial level.

3. Sealed Cover Submission: The report will be given in a sealed cover. This is often done in sensitive cases to ensure that the court is the first to review potentially contentious information, maintaining judicial integrity.

Why This Matters:

- Places of Worship Act, 1991: This act was meant to preserve the religious character of places as they existed on August 15, 1947. However, it doesn't apply to monuments protected by the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), like the Jama Masjid in Sambhal. This exception is crucial because it opens the door for legal scrutiny that wouldn't be possible under the Act's general protection.

- The Purpose of the Survey: The original case, filed by Advocate Vishnu Shankar Jain, aimed to determine the mosque's character. Now, with the survey report being submitted, it's about getting closer to answering this question. 

- Legal Implications: The Hindu side isn't viewing this as a victory for the Masjid side because the report's submission means the investigation into the mosque's origins and character will continue. The sealed cover ensures that the findings are preserved for judicial review before any public or media speculation.

What's Next?

- Trial Court's Role:*The trial court has a scheduled hearing on January 8. There's no rush to proceed until the Masjid Committee makes its move in the High Court, which could potentially challenge or affirm the survey.

- High Court's Potential Decision: Depending on how the Masjid Committee argues their case, the High Court could either validate the survey's continuation or find grounds to halt or alter the process.

The Broader Conversation:

This isn't just about a piece of land or a structure; it's about history, identity, and legal rights:

- Cultural Heritage: Every stone, every inscription, every architectural feature of a site like this could tell a story of a civilization. If there's evidence suggesting a different historical use of the site, that's a story that needs to be told, preserved, and understood.

- Religious Rights: The sanctity of places of worship is a sensitive topic. For communities, these are not just buildings but embodiments of faith. How do you balance the right to worship with the right to investigate historical claims?

- Legal Precedents: This case could set a precedent for how religious disputes over historical sites are handled in India, especially where ASI protection plays a role. It's a test of how the legal system can navigate through claims of history, archaeology, and religious sentiment.

- Political Undercurrents: Let's not ignore that such cases often have political dimensions. They can influence community relations, electoral politics, and even national security concerns.

Reflections:

- Transparency and Justice: The sealed cover ensures that the findings aren't tampered with or sensationalized before judicial review, promoting a form of transparency where justice is seen to be done by the court first.

- Community Dialogue: This is an opportunity for dialogue between communities. If handled with sensitivity, it could lead to a mutual understanding of history and coexistence.

- Educational Value: Whatever the outcome, this case is a lesson in how history, law, and religion can intersect in modern contexts, offering insights into how societies deal with their past.

While the Supreme Court's decision might seem procedural, it's a pivotal moment in a case that touches on deep historical, cultural, and religious issues. It's a moment for all of us to watch, learn from, and reflect upon. Let's hope that justice, in its truest form, prevails, ensuring that historical truths are respected alongside the rights and sentiments of all involved communities. Department slapped a belated GST notice and pursued parallel ITC inquiries against an Assessee; High Court quashes the demands, ruling that annual return extensions cannot extend limitation for the revenue and parallel proceedings violate Section 6(2)(b).

Issue:
Whether the Demand-cum-Show Cause Notice dated 22.07.2024 issued under Section 74(1) of the CGST Act for FY 2017-18 was barred by limitation under Section 74(10), despite statutory notifications extending return filing due dates. Whether the Central GST authorities were barred under Section 6(2)(b) of the CGST Act from initiating proceedings on excess Input Tax Credit (ITC) for FY 2018-19 and FY 2019-20 when the State GST authorities had already initiated proceedings on the identical subject matter.

Rule:
Section 74(10) of the CGST Act: Mandates that an adjudication order under Section 74(9) must be passed within five years from the due date of furnishing the annual return for the relevant financial year. Section 6(2)(b) of the CGST Act & M/s Armour Security (India) Ltd. (SC, 2025): Expressly bars the Department from initiating parallel adjudicatory proceedings on the "same subject matter" when the counterpart tax administration (Central or State) has already formally initiated proceedings by issuing a show cause notice. The statutory bar applies where two proceedings seek to assess or recover an identical or overlapping tax liability or contravention, though it does not restrict inquiries into distinct infractions. Section 168A of the CGST Act: Empowers the Government to extend statutory timelines under force majeure conditions; however, notifications extending taxpayer return compliance cannot be construed as extending the limitation period available to the Department for issuing notices under Section 74.

Application:
For FY 2017-18, the original due date for filing the annual return expired on 31.12.2018, though it was extended up to 07.02.2020 for the State of Tripura vide Notification No. 06/2020. On 22.03.2021, the Central GST authorities issued a preliminary scrutiny inquiry to the Assessee regarding an alleged deposit of VAT in the GST regime, which did not contain allegations of fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression. For FY 2018-19 and FY 2019-20, the State GST authorities issued show cause notices on 24.02.2025 concerning mismatches in ITC availed in the Electronic Credit Ledger versus the annual return; these proceedings were later dropped on 08.07.2025. Meanwhile, on 22.07.2024, the Central GST Department issued a composite Demand-cum-Show Cause Notice under Section 74(1) covering FY 2017-18, 2018-19, 2019-20, and 2020-21, raising demands for excess ITC and short payment of GST. On 03.02.2025, the Central GST Department adjudicated the notice and passed the Order-in-Original against the Assessee. The Assessee challenged the notice and the order before the High Court of Tripura via a writ petition.

Conclusion:
The High Court partly set aside the Demand-cum-Show Cause Notice dated 22.07.2024 to the extent it lacked jurisdiction (quashing the demands for FY 2017-18 and the excess ITC demands for FY 2018-19 and FY 2019-20). The Order-in-Original dated 03.02.2025 was quashed in its entirety. The matter was remitted to the Joint Commissioner for fresh adjudication strictly confined to the permissible surviving issues within three months, with liberty granted to the Assessee to file an additional reply challenging the invocation of Section 74 within six weeks.

Impact Analysis:
This ruling cements the rule that taxpayer-centric return extensions cannot be weaponised by the revenue to stretch limitation periods under Section 74, while firmly enforcing Section 6(2)(b) to protect assessees from dual, overlapping scrutiny by Central and State authorities on the same subject matter.

 What the Supreme Court settled there is different: after an order nisi, the lawful response is an affidavit or counter-affidavit to show cause, not a freestanding motion to set aside the order nisi; an allegation such as non-service must be positively deposed to; and a garnishee’s affidavit is limited to whether it holds an attachable debt.
So the proper course is to hear the counter-affidavit, or otherwise determine the issue it raises, before discharging any garnishee whose liability is contested in it. Discharge without that step is open to challenge as a denial of fair hearing and a failure to follow sections 86 and 87 Sheriffs Civil Processes Act.

text:
INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

Statement: MeitY’s “enhanced diligence” advisory pressures platforms to police protest speech. It must be withdrawn.

October 9, 2026

On October 8, MeitY’s Cyber Laws Division sent an advisory to all social media intermediaries. It asks them to exercise “enhanced diligence” over false, misleading, manipulated or out-of-context content linked to “ongoing public events and developments”, to “identify, prevent and not promote” unlawful information, to label or “contextualise” misleading content, and to prioritise complaints from “authorised Government agencies” on public-order content. It takes effect immediately. MeitY has not published it and its text became public through MediaNama. It was issued as citizens protest in Delhi and Mumbai over the revision of electoral rolls, with a protest called at Jantar Mantar for October 10. We call on MEITY to withdraw it.

First, the advisory names no provision that empowers MeitY to issue it and such advisories are not issued under any law. Section 79(2)(c) of the IT Act conditions safe harbour on “due diligence” and on guidelines the Central Government may “prescribe”, that is, by rules notified and laid before Parliament under Section 87. The IT Rules recognise only “due diligence” under Rule 3 and “additional due diligence” for significant social media intermediaries under Rule 4. The phrase, “Enhanced diligence” used in this Advisory appears in neither. Further, MeitY’s proposed Rule 3(4) in the last round of Amendments mooted to the IT Rules, 2021, which has not been notified further confirms this does not have any legal character. Second, an advisory cannot alter the application of existing law. Rule 3(1)(b)(v) covers only misinformation communicated “knowingly and intentionally” that is “patently false and untrue or misleading in nature”. The advisory drops both qualifiers and adds “social tranquility”, neither that nor “misleading” is a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).

Third, facing an undefined standard platforms will censor more than the law requires. The advisory asks them to “identify, prevent and not promote” unlawful information and to “strengthen their existing monitoring”. This is proactive monitoring by another name, which the Rules contemplate only for narrow categories such as child sexual abuse material. Further, it is vague and does does not define “authorised Government agencies” or “priority”, and does not require platforms to tell users that a government complaint lay behind an action. Users will see only a platform decision. The State’s role disappears, and with it any route to challenge that role in court. The advisory governs public speech but is not itself public. It cites no statutory provision, is approved by an unnamed “competent authority”, and does not identify the events or content that prompted it.

We anticipate a huge spike in censorship over the next few days.

We call on MeitY to:
1. Publish the advisory in full, including any clause (v), and state the provision under which it was issued.
2. Withdraw it, or clarify that it creates no obligations beyond the IT Act and Rules and that “enhanced diligence” is not a condition of safe harbour.
3. Disclose which agencies are sending complaints under it, and how many.
4. Abandon the proposed Rule 3(4).

We also call on platforms to:
1. Disclose all government complaints and requests received under this advisory.
2. Act only on requests that meet the Shreya Singhal standard and Rule 3(1)(d).
3. Refrain from proactively filtering or downranking protest content on the basis of this advisory.
4. Notify affected users, including when an action follows a government complaint.

Report: White House Fears UK Apple iCloud Backdoor Targets Trump, Farage | Ken Macon, Reclaim The Net

The New Statesman is reporting that a White House security official expects the UK to use the backdoor it wants to build into Apple's iCloud – through a secret court order – to spy on the Trump administration and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

The magazine said it had seen a message sent in September from the official to a colleague, which reads: "The UK is making another attempt to put a backdoor on iCloud. This time by their secret court. They're going to lean on a court order to justify it. They will use this back door to spy on the administration and Nigel Farage."

The report does not show that anyone has actually been spied on in this way, and it's obviously alarmist, but the message reveals the fear is present inside the US administration, so at least people are aware of what the UK is doing to undermine privacy.

It is also a perfect example of how a backdoor built to catch criminals is actually a tool that can be used by whoever happens to have it at their disposal, including against political opponents – and allies.

The UK is keeping the order so secret that Apple was able to brief the US Vice President about it - but not the US Congress.

The UK first tried to get Apple to give it access to all iCloud users' encrypted cloud backups around the world, through the country's Investigatory Powers Act, and a secret technical capability notice (TCN). The order was later changed to cover only UK users, after the US put pressure on its ally.

Apple never built that backdoor, at least as far as we know. Instead, it withdrew its strongest encryption, Advanced Data Protection, from UK users, and new UK users are still unable to turn it on.

Apple has also said that it has "never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products and services and never will."

In June, House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan wrote to UK Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood to warn that if reports about the UK order were true, it would mean that the country is building "backdoors into their encrypted services."

Jordan said that would put at risk the security of US citizens' data.

In September, Democratic Senator Ron Wyden and Republican Representative Warren Davidson wrote to the UK’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal to express their concern over the secret order, saying that the UK was being “wholly inappropriate” in preventing Apple from discussing the issue with US Congress.

"The U.K. government's unprecedented demands for secrecy in this matter undermine democratic governance in both the United States and the U.K., and needlessly strain the relationship between our two nations," the two congressmen wrote.

Weakening encryption in consumer software, the letter said, “introduces critical vulnerabilities that can be exploited by hostile foreign actors.”

Apple went to the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT), which hears complaints about surveillance, to try to have the UK order revoked. Privacy International and Liberty have a separate challenge before the same court.

The UK government will neither confirm nor deny that the order exists. But Ben Jaffey KC, who represents Privacy International and Liberty, told the tribunal that "the horse has long bolted."

"The fact that Apple even needed to ask permission confirms there is a TCN," Jaffey said.

Meanwhile, Neil Sheldon KC, acting for the government, said the home secretary's position was "neither irrational nor unsupported by evidence."

In February 2025, Reclaim The Net reported that the UK was trying to force Apple to give it access to all iCloud users' encrypted cloud backups around the world, and that Apple had in the meantime pulled its strongest encryption, Advanced Data Protection, from UK users.

In September 2025, we reported that Farage had told the US Congress that the UK's Online Safety Act was a threat not only to free speech, but also to encryption.

In June, we reported about Jordan's letter to Mahmood, warning that the UK order could compromise data of US citizens.

A backdoor does not check who is asking to use it, or why – and the officials worried about it being turned on Farage and the Trump administration are essentially describing why nobody should have a backdoor.
