I've spent years in C and C++ at Microsoft and Google, and I've reviewed thousands of changes. I've watched good engineers ship bad code because the reviewer skimmed it, approved it, and went to lunch.

Now AI writes code 200× faster. Who reviews it?

If you're not enforcing strict 3-engineer code reviews on every change before it ships, you have no business building software.

Kidding. That was true yesterday.

Today I'm going to answer whether AI can review AI-generated code. Then I'll show you how to get an outstanding, senior-level review that doesn't miss details, for under a dollar a review.

Bookmark this. The full REVIEW.md is in the first reply, ready to paste.

The results surprised me

1/ I asked the AI session that wrote the code to review its own work. It found only 3 of 23 issues and recommended merging. Then I started a brand-new agent on the same model, with no memory of writing the code, and gave it only the diff. It found 17 of 23.

2/ Reviewers that only read the code found zero of the 8 logic bugs in the feature PR. Every logic bug was found by a reviewer that ran the code.

3/ One rule added to the reviewer's instructions took it from 4 of 8 logic bugs to 7 of 8, plus one nobody had found. Same model, $0.72 → $0.74, 27% faster.

4/ The most expensive model wasn't the best deal. Opus matched or beat Fable on both PRs at about a third of the price: under $1 a review vs. over $2.

5/ The next day, a brand-new reviewer agent found 4 blocking bugs in a PR with 272 passing tests and green CI.

6/ "Always get a code review" was written into the agent's instructions, and the agent skipped it on the very first PR.

It's an incredible unlock. No more bugs sailing through on a green checkmark.

Here's how I got there.

The setup

• 2 real PRs from a production codebase. One was a 75-file refactor, the other a 23-file feature.
• 12 reviews in total: 4 by an AI session that already had context on the work, 8 by brand-new agents that had only the diff, the repo and a rules file.
• 3 models: Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5.
• I re-ran every reported defect myself, on the PR and on today's head, to sort live bugs from fixed ones.
• Costs are estimated from each reviewer's token count at API list prices, with no caching discount, so they lean high.

Then I put it to work on a real feature. That case study is below.

1. Context is the blind spot, not authorship.

On the refactor:
• The session that wrote the code, reviewing its own work (Fable): found only 3 of 23 issues
• A brand-new Fable agent, with no memory of the work: found 17 of 23
• A brand-new Opus agent: found 18 of 23

On the feature PR, written by a different session three days earlier:
• A Fable session that hadn't written it but had spent a day working in this repo: found 0 of 8 logic bugs
• Brand-new Fable, Opus and Sonnet agents: found 2 to 4 of 8 each

The feature-PR reviewer didn't write the code, and it still found nothing. A reviewer that shares the writer's mental model inherits the writer's blind spots, whoever wrote the code.

2. Reading finds style problems. Running the code finds bugs.

Every logic bug came from a reviewer that built a throwaway database, called the changed code with inputs it picked itself, and watched what came back. The session that already had context ran nothing. It read the code and found no logic bugs.

None of the 8 logic bugs on the feature PR are visible from the diff text alone. Every one of them is obvious once you run the code.

3. A rules file did almost nothing for the reviewer with context.

Giving it a written checklist added one finding per PR. Logic bugs found: still zero. With the same file, brand-new Fable and Opus agents found 13 to 18 issues per PR. A checklist can't fix a reviewer that already believes the code is correct.

4. The failure was in the order the reviewer worked.

The best brand-new reviewer still missed half the logic bugs, so I pulled its full tool-call trace and went through it step by step.

It had opened the functions behind all three bugs it missed, and it understood each one. But it wrote its test inputs after reading the implementation, so every input followed the implementation's own assumptions. Its edge cases were variations on the cases the code already handled.

The code had effectively written its own exam, and it passed.

The fix was one rule: "Write your test inputs before you read the implementation. Then run them." Same model, same PR: recall went from 4 of 8 to 7 of 8, plus a bug nobody had found, for two cents more.

5. The model matters, but less than the process.

Opus 5.5: $0.72 to $0.93 per review, 8 to 11 minutes. It found the most issues on both PRs: the best balance of thoroughness and cost.

Fable 5.1: $2.11 to $2.73, about 3× Opus. Found a bug nobody else caught on each PR, but skipped the base-branch comparison when the tests were green.

Sonnet 5.5: $0.14 to $0.21. The cheapest per finding, but it found 2 of 8, then 4 of 8 on the identical input. That run-to-run variance is the real cost.

The two strongest reviewers overlapped on only 10 of 20 findings.

A surprising case study: one real feature, reviewed end to end

An agent built a real feature: 37 files, 5,000+ lines of code, 272 tests passing, CI green. It pushed without a review.

I made it get one.

11 major bugs. A brand-new Opus reviewer found 11 blocking bugs, plus dozens of smaller issues. Every one of them was behind a green checkmark.

8 reviews, 6 rounds of fixes. Each cycle was review → fix → review again:
• The feature: 4 blockers → fix → approved, but that fix broke a filter → fix → approved. That's 3 reviews.
• The tool that enforces review: 4 blockers → fix → 2 more → fix → 1 more → fix → approved → small fix → approved. That's 5 reviews.

It all took under 40 minutes, at under a dollar per review.

What would have shipped without review:
• Every page of the new feature would crash on Feb 29.
• Users would see records labelled with a premium category they didn't belong to.
• A list would show stale data whenever a user changed a filter.
• A crafted link could slip hidden recipients into an email the user sends.
• The review gate wouldn't have enforced review: it checked the wrong repo and let real pushes through.
• Worse, installing it would have silently switched off every safety check that already ran on each commit.
• A database file would have been committed to the repo.

What this case taught me:

1/ 272 passing tests said nothing about these bugs. None of them had a test.

2/ The first approval wasn't the end. A fix for one bug created another, and only the second review caught it.

3/ The tool that enforces review needed 3 rounds of changes before it worked. Review the gate, not just the code.

Best practices for your AI code reviewer

1/ Always start a brand-new agent with no memory of writing the code. Give it only the diff, the repo and REVIEW.md. On the same model, this took recall from 3 of 23 to 17 of 23.

2/ Make it run the code, not just read it. Reading found zero logic bugs; every logic bug came from running the code.

3/ Have it write its test inputs before it reads the implementation. This one rule took recall from 4 of 8 to 7 of 8 for two cents more.

4/ Compare test results against the base branch every time, even when everything is green.

5/ Re-review every fix commit. Fixes create bugs.

6/ Use Opus by default. Add a second reviewer on a different model for business rules, thresholds and gates. The two best reviewers overlapped on only half their findings.

7/ Enforce review with a gate, not a prompt. Use a git pre-push hook: no approved review for that exact commit, no push. Edits to the rules themselves get reviewed too.

8/ Make it report on every design principle by name: separation of concerns, programming by intention, encapsulation, high cohesion, low coupling. A principle left unmentioned means the review is incomplete.

9/ Check honesty, not just style. Unknown stays unknown. The UI never invents data.

10/ Demand a clear verdict (APPROVE or CHANGES) and report findings as "N of the K found so far." The bug pool is never complete.

The full REVIEW.md is in the reply below Paste it into your repo and point your review agent at it.

REVIEW.md: rules for AI code review. Paste this into your repo.

1. WHO REVIEWS
• The reviewer is a fresh agent that did NOT write the code. It gets only: the diff, the repo, this file.
• The writer's self-review is a checklist pass, not a review.
• Default model: Opus. High-risk changes (business rules, thresholds, scoring, pricing, validation gates) get a second reviewer on a different model.
• Every fix commit gets its own review. Fixes create bugs.

2. HOW TO REVIEW: EXECUTE, DON'T READ
• Before reading the implementation, write down the inputs you will test. Inputs written after reading the code take the code's shape and miss what it misses.
• Run the changed code on those inputs, in a throwaway environment. Where possible, probe read-only against a copy of real data.
• Compare test results against the base commit every time, including when the head is green.

3. WHAT TO PROBE
• Every alternative form of an input, including forms that combine two of them.
• Every unit, and the input with no unit at all.
• Two or more entities in one input, in every order.
• Every consumer of a changed enum, status or constant.
• Every reason or error code, traced to the message the user actually sees.
• Every place the same fact is stored, computed or rendered (server and client). Do they still agree?
• Boundaries: empty, one, exactly-at-threshold, past the top.
• Dates: leap days, year boundaries, time zones.

4. HONESTY
• Unknown stays unknown. The UI never invents, guesses or silently resolves data it does not have.
• Every label must be true for every record it is shown on.

5. DESIGN PRINCIPLES (REPORT ON EVERY ONE)
For each: OK, or a violation with file:line.
• Separation of concerns
• Programming by intention
• Encapsulation
• High cohesion
• Low coupling
Blocking: a domain with two owners, duplicated logic, business logic in templates or UI code.
A principle left unmentioned = an incomplete review.

6. GATES AND TOOLING
• Attack every new check, hook or gate with inputs it should reject, including ones phrased differently to evade it.
• Prefer platform primitives (e.g. git pre-push) over clever parsing of commands.
• Confirm every exemption still points at something that exists, and that no exemption can be used to sneak code through.
• Installing a hook must not disable hooks already in place.
• Edits to the rules themselves are never exempt from review.

7. DOCS AND REFACTORS
• After any search-and-replace or move, re-read every edited sentence and ask: is this still true?
• Dated docs keep their old paths and facts.

8. REPORTING
• Findings are BLOCKING or NIT. Blocking must be fixed; nits are optional.
• Each finding gets a reproduction: input, expected, actual.
• Report "N of the K found so far." The pool is never complete.
• Green tests are not evidence. Say what you executed.
• End with exactly one line: VERDICT: APPROVE or VERDICT: CHANGES

The Silent Emergency: Eleven Years Under the Shadow of Control

India, the land of a billion vibrant voices, is grappling with a chilling silence. For eleven years under the PM, we've witnessed an

"Undeclared Emergency@11"

—no declared curfews, no tanks, but a steady erosion of our democratic freedoms. This is the story of a Nation fighting for its soul, where the cost of speaking out grows heavier daily.

The Press in Chains
Our Fourth Estate, once a beacon of truth, now falters under relentless pressure. V-Dem and Freedom House 2025 reports label India an “electoral autocracy,” ranked “partly free.” The Press Freedom Index places us at 159/176, near Somalia’s shadow. Honest journalists face arrests, raids, and intimidation for daring to question. Laws like UAPA and sedition are weaponized, branding critics “terrorists” without trial. Media houses face raids, their voices stifled. Modi’s 11-year tenure without a single press conference speaks volumes—hate speech thrives, but truth is jailed.

Homes Turned to Rubble
Bulldozers roar across India, not for progress but as tools of vengeance. Homes, often of minorities or dissenters, are demolished in displays of state power. Families stand amid rubble, targeted for their identity or beliefs. Ministers spewing hate are rewarded, while citizens live in fear. This isn’t the India we fought for.

The Digital Gag
In the age of X, FB, Insta, and YouTube, where voices once soared, dissent is now caged. Content creators and tweeters face arrests for “misinformation” or “inciting unrest.” Over 20,000 independent voices have been silenced, their crime often a post challenging the regime. This is a democracy where keyboards are as dangerous as megaphones.

Opposition Under Siege
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has become a weapon to intimidate opposition leaders, with raids targeting those who refuse to bow to the BJP. Homes and offices of opposition figures are stormed, cases piled up to coerce them into joining the ruling party or face relentless harassment. This blatant misuse of agencies undermines democracy, turning dissent into a dangerous act.

Puppet Election Commission
The Election Commission, once a pillar of democratic integrity, now dances to the tune of the BJP. The removal of the Chief Justice of India from the selection committee for appointing Election Commissioners has raised alarms about its independence. This move, critics argue, ensures a pliable EC, ready to tilt the electoral scales. Free and fair elections, the heartbeat of democracy, now pulse under the shadow of control.

The Leader’s Shadow
Modi’s image dominates—billboards, screens, even vaccine certificates and rail tickets. Supporters call it leadership; we see a cult stifling dissent. Parliament weakened, constitutional bodies eroded, divisive figures glorified—this is a five-fold assault on our democracy. BJP invokes 1975’s Emergency to deflect, but today’s control needs no formal name. It’s a slow, silent strangulation of our freedoms.

Nation’s Resolve
Fifty years ago, India resisted the 1975 Emergency. Today, the shackles are subtler but real. Jailed journalists, bulldozed homes, silenced voices, ED raids on opposition leaders, and a compromised Election Commission tell of a democracy under siege. As Modi marks “Samvidhan Hatya Diwas,” we say the real threat to our Constitution is now—unnamed, insidious, but ever-present.

India stands at a crossroads. Will we reclaim our chorus of voices or let silence prevail? The fight for our democracy lies in the courage of those who speak, write, and dream of a free tomorrow.

text:
Before calling Indians insecure nationalists, perhaps understand the issue you are commenting on.

India is not obligated to wave Musk through its regulatory system simply because he promises connectivity. Starlink is a commercial satellite network, not a charitable mission, and India has every right to scrutinise the technology, business model and security implications before allowing it to operate.

First, national security is not an inconvenience to be dismissed. Satellite networks operate across borders. India must establish how Indian traffic will be routed, how lawful interception will work, whether data and gateways remain under effective Indian jurisdiction, and whether services can be restricted during emergencies. These are legitimate questions of sovereignty, particularly in a country with sensitive borders and active security challenges. India’s own licensing framework requires compliance with security conditions, lawful interception and domestic gateway requirements. 

Second, connectivity does not automatically mean affordability. Starlink requires specialised user terminals, satellite infrastructure and recurring subscription payments. It may be invaluable in remote villages, mountainous regions, disaster zones and areas where terrestrial networks are uneconomical. But it is not self-evidently the cheapest solution for millions of ordinary Indians when mobile broadband and fibre already serve vast parts of the country. The real question is where satellite internet fills a genuine gap, at what cost, and for whom.

Third, spectrum is a public resource, not Elon Musk’s private entitlement. Its allocation, pricing and conditions must account for national security, efficient use, fair competition and the interests of existing telecom networks. India has a regulatory process for precisely these reasons. 

Fourth, the conspiracy allegation itself deserves scrutiny. As of October 2026, the government says Starlink, Jio and OneWeb are at broadly similar stages of security assessment. All have received preliminary approvals, but further clearances and spectrum arrangements remain necessary. That does not prove every delay is justified, and the government should be held accountable for unreasonable delays. But it certainly does not establish that Indian oligarchs are secretly conspiring to block Musk. 

And let us address your personal insult. Questioning Musk’s allegation is not the same as worshipping Indian billionaires. If Ambani or Mittal receives preferential treatment, expose it. If regulators are deliberately delaying Starlink, produce the evidence. But do not demand that Indians accept an unsubstantiated accusation merely because its author is a billionaire selling a blue tick.

As for democracy, India conducts elections on an extraordinary scale through EVMs with VVPAT paper trails. The United States has a decentralised patchwork of voting systems, and its Capitol was attacked on January 6, 2021, in an attempt to disrupt the constitutional transfer of power. Neither fact makes one country infallible or the other illegitimate. The point is simple: no country gets to claim moral superiority while demanding that others abandon critical scrutiny.

And no, this is not about wounded national pride. It is about refusing to confuse corporate lobbying with public service.

India welcomes technology. India needs competition. India needs better connectivity in underserved areas. Starlink may well contribute to all three.

But India also needs security, affordable access, fair regulation and sovereign control over critical infrastructure.

A billionaire’s commercial ambitions aren’t constitutional rights. Allegations aren’t evidence, and questioning Musk doesn’t make 1.4 billion Indians stupid or insecure.

Learn the difference between defending a monopoly and defending India’s sovereign right to set rules for every company, Indian or foreign.

STATEMENT OF SOLIDARITY WITH THE YOUTH OF INDIA

Dhaka, Bangladesh | 10 October 2026

To the youth and democratic forces of India,

We stand in firm solidarity with the young people of India demanding electoral accountability and defending their democratic rights. Recent detentions of peaceful protesters, organizers, and journalists in New Delhi, alongside internet suspensions and restrictions at Jantar Mantar, directly threaten fundamental freedoms. Concerns regarding electoral integrity and institutional independence require transparent answers, not barricades and censorship.

This struggle is not yours alone. From Dhaka, we stand with you as friends bound by a common demand for accountable power, democratic institutions, and human dignity.

We know this struggle intimately, because we have lived it. In July 2024, our student led movement against recruitment quotas transformed into a nationwide uprising against 15 years of authoritarian rule. The state responded with live ammunition. The United Nations later estimated that as many as 1,400 people were killed during the uprising and its suppression. We deeply remember and honor the solidarity shown by Indian students, writers, and independent voices during our uprising.

We recognize India's rich traditions of democratic resistance. The women of Shaheen Bagh defended equal citizenship through a Delhi winter, while generations of students at JNU and Jadavpur University have sustained organised dissent. These remain invaluable democratic inheritances. Today, we once again see the courage of young Indian women on the streets. In Bangladesh, women were also at the forefront of the July Revolution; their courage and sacrifices helped secure our victory.

Hindutva majoritarianism, fascism, and every form of religious supremacy must not define the future of South Asia. We reject authoritarianism, communal hatred, and political intolerance in India just as we reject them in Bangladesh. Our shared future must rest on communal harmony and social justice, irrespective of religion, caste, gender, or class. No society is truly democratic while minorities live in fear, dissent is criminalized, and citizenship is conditional on identity.

We call upon Indian authorities to respect the right to peaceful assembly, disclose the whereabouts and legal grounds for detaining protest organizers, immediately release those held for exercising their rights, and ensure journalists can report without intimidation or equipment seizure.

Today, many young leaders have been unjustly detained. Sharjeel Imam and Umar Khalid continue to be kept behind bars for years without trial. We regard all of India's young protesters and prisoners of conscience as comrades. Their courage inspires young people across South Asia.

Our struggles are interconnected, extending to unresolved issues of border killings, water sharing, environmental protection, and national sovereignty. We seek a South Asia where nations treat each other as equals, governments remain accountable, and sovereignty is never an excuse for domination.

To the democratic people of India: from Dhaka, and from the unfinished democratic aspirations of our July generation, we stand with you. Stand firm, protect one another, reject communal hatred, and refuse to surrender the future of South Asia to fascism and division.

Breaking :

EU Council wants to abolish correspondence secrecy

The EU member states want to abolish the modern secrecy of letters. In  the EU Council, the police should be able to prosecute private chat  flows and monitor such a letter communication. Experts warn that Signal  and WhatsApp could leave the EU.

The EU of citizens' rights – has this combination of words already  been heard? But the EU of governments, which is well there. The  elections in Belgium were held in parallel with the EU elections on 9.  held in June and ended with a triumph for the Flemish right-wing  conservatives (N-VA) and the Vlaams Belang. Liberal Prime Minister  Alexander De Croo immediately declared his resignation, but remains in  office. Its centre-left coalition will probably not be once again after  the losses suffered.

But now the country could end up one last coup in EU Brussels. Until  the 1. The Belgian Government holds the semi-annual Presidency of the EU  Council in July. Since the beginning of the year, the De Croo  government has been trying to enforce general chat control in the EU,  especially at end-to-end encrypted services such as WhatsApp or Signal.  EU bodies have been planning this advance for a long time. So far, there  have been one or two vetoos too much in the Council. But now France had  itself break out of the blocking minority. And so the Belgian proposal  could already be adopted in the Council on Wednesday.

The Regulation includes the title of "Rules to combat child abuse".  It is supposedly about images that record child abuse (child sexual  abuse material, CSAM), and also sent internet links should be scanned  automatically. Ultimately, it is about access to the online  communication of citizens. The laudable fight against child pornography  is the giant hammer, with which the small nail data protection and the  right to privacy for all citizens are to be sunk into the ground.
An increase in security is not expected

“Send me a Whatsapp,” you hear (still) everywhere. Many citizens use  the chat apps every day, almost self-evident, of course, also send a  picture, a meme, an Internet link. Three quarters of 16- to 74 year olds  across the EU are registered with one of the various apps such as  Skype, Telegram, Threema, etc. In Germany, 60 million alone use the  WhatsApp chat service, which has been part of the Facebook Group Meta  for some time. Since that is the case, many have been looking for  alternatives because Facebook is considered a data vacuum cleaner with  partly dubary terms of use. Now the EU wants to put it equally on the  Big Tech Group and gain insight into the private communication of the  citizens, block it or prosecute it in the event of a case. The country  bloc seizes the technical services and becomes the imitator of the large  tech companies, which it should actually include in the sense of the  freedom of its citizens.

If the EU regulation comes, app users will probably see one of these  windows at some point. In it, they are asked whether they agree to  verify their sent images, photos and videos by artificial intelligence  (AI) or not. If not, they will no longer be able to use the service or  at least not send any pictures, etc. However, it is likely that many  will agree with the new terms of use almost otherwise – and so the EU  would come a little closer to the comprehensive control of its citizens.

Those who have something to hide will simply not agree to the new  conditions and use darker channels, as they do today. So there would be  no increase in security for small children who fall victim to sexual  abuse and whose images are then spread. Ultimately, the EU regulation  amounts to suspend mass surveillance of citizens and thus possible  prosecution even where there is no plaintiff. For example, where  teenagers send lewd pictures. And AI can, of course, become erred and  possibly classify harmless content as potentially dangerous.
Legal service of the Council: Arbitrary control violates fundamental rights

Initially, even the checking of the chat messages and recorded voice  messages was planned on keywords. These are individual regulations that  were withdrawn for the first, according to the former MEP Patrick Breyer  (Pirates). In addition, France has returned a derogation for security  authorities and military, which can then continue to send pictures and  videos without these being subjected to any kind of scanning.

The Legal Service of the Council was still in force on 24. May found  that "arbitrary chat control" is still on the EU agenda for persons who  are not suspected of committing a crime and, of course, constitute a  violation of fundamental rights (in Germany Article 13 of the Basic  Law).

If the regulation comes, private chat providers can no longer keep  one of their most important promises. Signal’s president, Meredith  Whittaker, writes in a recent press release that “upload moderation” is  only a new word for mass chat control: “There is no way to implement  such proposals related to end-to-end encrypted communication without  fundamentally undermining encryption and creating a dangerous weakness  in a core infrastructure that would have a global impact far beyond  Europe.”

The claim that content is still being “checked before” its encryption  is contrary to the end-to-end principle with which WhatsApp and signal  promote itself. Signal had once developed open source technology,  WhatsApp took it over, Mark Zuckerberg has not yet touched it. According  to Whittaker, encryption and “upload moderation” do not go together –  this is an “mathematical reality” that new words could not hide either.  The EU chat control proposal is about “mass scanning” about “the same  old monitoring with a new label” using “mass scanning”.

One thing goes without saying that if the chat services were to know  about “illegal activities” due to the surveillance of image content and  Internet addresses, they would not only have to inform the EU state or  supranational authorities immediately about it, but also “act quickly to  remove or block access to access it”. The AI-supported detection of  supposedly illegal content would therefore also result in its deletion.
Whittaker: We are previously leaving the EU market

Already in May, Whittaker announced that he would rely on the EU  market rather than engage in an undermining of encryption technology.  Now Signal has remained a niche provider with 40 million users  worldwide.

In addition to the head of the Signal, the Society for Freedom Rights also protest the organisation European Digital Rights (entitled “Be scanned – or get banned!”) and the Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT) Europe strongly against the draft regulation of the Belgian Presidency.

However, even the industry giant WhatsApp recently threatened with  its retirement from India within 60 days, according to the trade  magazines Rest of World and Inside Digital.  The government had previously adopted a regulation requiring  significant services (those with more than five million users) to  disclose the first author of information. With half a billion users in  India, WhatsApp belongs to this category, similar to what is a “very  large platform” under the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA) and is  therefore subject to EU censorship law. Due to the importance of  WhatsApp for the Indian economy, a compromise is expected.

In the EU, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Austria and Poland  have been against the plans. Now the Belgians were apparently able to  capture France through the concession for security services and the  military. The blocking minority in the Council could therefore tip this  Wednesday. It is frightening that the conditions in the EU Council have  become so scarce that a majority is tangible. Estonia, Finland, Greece,  Italy, Portugal, Sweden, Slovenia and the Czech Republic have not yet  determined.

The European Parliament in Strasbourg-Brussels spoke out in November  to maintain chat encryption. If the Council decision is taken on  Wednesday, then perhaps the hour of this Parliament could really beat:  it would then have to do everything possible to prevent chat control in  the so-called 'trilogue' of the three EU institutions.

Bitchat, the messaging app made by Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey, has been removed from app stores in India.

Bitchat does not need the internet or a mobile network. Phones close to each other pass messages along over Bluetooth, so it keeps working even during an internet shutdown. Messages are encrypted and there is no central server.

The IT ministry ordered the removal on 3 October under Section 69A of the IT Act, the law the government uses to block websites and apps. The app is gone from Apple's App Store and Google Play in India, and its website does not open on many Indian internet providers.

In July, authorities had already asked GitHub to take down its code. The reason given then was that police cannot easily intercept or trace messages on it, and that it works during shutdowns.

India made up about 85% of all Bitchat downloads in one week of July, up from about 1% the month before.

The Internet Freedom Foundation, a digital rights group, says the law allows blocking unlawful content, not blocking an app because it works during shutdowns.

Michael.

He watched carefully until he was sure it was gone.

Unknown Number.

“Hello?” 

There was silence.

Then a man's voice whispered:
“Why did you delete my number?”

My heart stopped.
Because I recognized the voice.
It was Michael.

The same man Daniel had just told me to delete.

And then Michael said something that made me realize Daniel had lied to me about something.

“Your boyfriend knows exactly who I am.”

text:
I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

The IT Minister, Mr. Vaishnaw, announced that a consultation paper on AI regulation is a month away. Why even bother? 

It is eleven months since MeitY unveiled the India AI Governance Guidelines. Drafted by a committee the Ministry itself constituted, the Guidelines offered seven “sutras”, one helpfully titled “Innovation over Restraint”, counselled regulators against compliance heavy requirements, and left new laws for the long term. Now, as per Mr. Vaishnaw, the time for regulation has come. What time exactly? When did the clock strike cuckoo? Perhaps it was around the time of the last cabinet meeting.

But more seriously, what explains this lack of foresight? While a charitable commentator may put it down to the accelerated rate of AI development, the fault rests in the institutional culture of MEITY, which lacks seriousness and competence. This is a pattern evident across multiple consultations that I have participated in, in which the only ones which have resulted in any change are those which have led to changes in the IT Rules, 2021, where the censorship powers of the government have been expanded. The rest are mere PDF tigers that remain unimplemented as their visibility fades after a week of their release.

For instance, let’s ask some questions on the AI Governance Guidelines. Has an honest effort even been made at implementation? Where are the risk classification framework, the regulatory gap analysis and the master circular that the action plan promised in the short term, and who has assessed whether voluntary compliance failed? After all, as per the press release, more than 2,500 comments were received. This is the same result several other consultations have faced.

If MeitY wishes to consult, it should release a white paper on its primary task and role, which is to be the custodian and executioner of India’s Digital Censorship Infrastructure.  That is the only consultation which actually matters as it has fretted away India's technological lead over the past 12 years by reducing itself as a political censor. 

Now, for a second, let me assume some intelligence within MeitY. Two top priorities based on how it operates exist. First, perhaps this new AI consultation is actually aimed at censorship itself, emerging from more citizens mocking the Prime Minister and opposition parties using AI generated videos as crucial state elections heat up social media.  Or, maybe, this exercise may be little more than a retributive stratagem to place pressure on American AI companies, and through them on the economic interests of the United States? These fetched schemes presumes the ability of MEITY to form coherent thoughts, if not a solid plan, in the Ministry’s functioning, where both on planning and execution it fails consistently. 

So here comes another consultation. Most likely to lead to another forgotten file alongside the hundred others in my downloads folder.

Somewhere in 1945, at the dead of the night, the British intelligence intercepted a suspicious-looking seagoing trawler near the coast of Mumbai. A team of police raided the trawler but could find only kitchen utensils and gunny bags. The trawler was travelling from Yangon in Myanmar and the cargo belonged to a Gujarati engineer, B. C. Mehta. As soon as the trawler reached the coast Mehta took all the bags and utensils with him and went straight to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.

Why would a man coming from Yangon take those insignificant utensils and gunny bags to one of the tallest leaders of the Indian freedom struggle? 

Mehta was, in fact, on a very important mission. The mission was to tell the tales of bravery of valour displayed by Azad Hind Fauj on the battle field. Those gunny bags were hiding reels of a documentary film made by the propaganda unit of Fauj.

When Fauj led by Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose started suffering reverses in the war it was felt that Indians living in India needed to know the real story of Netaji. The British government had put severe censors on any news of Azad Hind Fauj. Indians were fed with a narrative that Netaji was a Japanese agent and Fauj was nothing but the Indian Japanese Fighting Force formed to establish Japanese colonialism in India. Though Fauj had a propaganda unit, its penetration into the Indian mainland was not much.

The propaganda unit of Fauj on the orders of Netaji made a documentary film that showed Netaji, soldiers on the battlefield, Rani Jhansi regiment, and other engagements of Fauj. Netaji might have left India after bitter differences with Mahatma Gandhi but he still had his sympathizers and allies in the Indian National Congress. These pro-Netaji leaders were contacted so that the film could be shown to the Indian public.

Mehta was a Gujarati engineer belonging to a business family who would, several times, drive Netaji in his vehicle in Myanmar. Sardar Patel was contacted by Azad Hind Fauj regarding this film. He pledged his support to smuggle the film into India and Mehta was given the responsibility to bring it into Indian territory.

Sardar Patel took the reels of the film with him and rushed to New Delhi. The film needed to be watched by all the senior Congress leaders. Patel asked Congress activists to arrange for a public screening of the film. Rajeshwar Dayal, owner of Regal Cinema at Connaught Place, was requested to allow screening at his theatre. He agreed and screening was arranged.

On the scheduled day Sardar Patel, Jawahar Lal Nehru, Maulana Azad, and each of the members of the Congress High Command watched the film. The outlook towards Azad Hind Fauj and Netaji was changed. People realized that Netaji was on a national mission to free his motherland and evil propaganda of the British that he was a Japanese agent was a lie. Gautam Kaul writes, “The film showed sequences of the members of Azad Hind Fauj training in the jungle and also the work of Rani of Jhansi Brigade of Indian women based in Yangon and Singapore. It also featured Bose moving around on inspection and meeting with other leaders of the region as well as exhorting his workers to prepare themselves for a long march to Delhi.”

After the screening, as expected, Dayal received a notice from the government for violating the law. Rajinder Narain, who also argued at the famous Red Fort INA trials, was asked by Dayal to help him. Narain took him to Kunwar Mohinder Singh Bedi, who was the city magistrate then, and asked for his help. Bedi knew how to help a patriot within the ambit of colonial law. After the first hearing, he declared a long vacation. He did not list the case for hearings until India got independence.

Important update. https://t.co/YBTKIgkyZP has been taken down.

After months of building this initiative for mass adoption across India (feeding it nationwide PM-to-ward-level representative data) and getting very close to public release, I received a notice from MeitY
My DNS was eventually taken down ( it's been 45 days). The concern raised was that I was using photos and information of ministers and public representatives for features such as Certificate of Shame and Leader Geotag photos.

I’m currently working through the issue with the authorities. But I also have another plan to relaunch this.

Before I reveal it, here’s what makes this project fundamentally different and why taking down a single website doesn’t actually take down the application.
I built the entire application on the Internet Computer #ICP  blockchain. The application logic and data live on-chain.

The app is still accessible through its native blockchain URL, but that URL isn’t human-friendly. So I connected it to a Web2 domain: https://t.co/ihjT4pIcBF.

The government can block the Web2 domain but they can't simply "take down" the application that exists on the blockchain.

And this highlights one of the biggest missing pieces of the decentralized web: on-chain DNS.

The ICP ecosystem is already moving in this direction, with the broader vision around DNSSEC, NNS and Chain-Key technology. ( @dominic_w @PierreSamaties
Any update on this? )

Until that becomes practical, I have two options: 1. Launch under another Web2 domain.
2. Work with an NGO/organization that can provide a more resilient layer for access, while staying within legal boundaries.

More soon.
@malpani  @DefenceBrat @dfinity

My Facebook account was restricted in India on July 2. The notice shown by Meta refers to a Government of India / Law Enforcement request.

But the bigger concern is the pattern... voices questioning the Revanth Reddy government are facing restrictions, while my account remains blocked even after the Telangana High Court passed an interim order in my favour nearly 20 days ago.

I contacted Meta Customer Support to submit the court order. I was told there is no Meta Legal Cell in India and that the order should be sent directly to Meta in the US. Other India-related Meta email addresses have also received no response.

There is information that Meta’s legal representative may have appeared before the High Court, though I cannot independently confirm the exact details.

And now, Telugu Scribe has reportedly faced a similar restriction today.

If the Revanth Reddy government is using such methods to deal with people who question it, this is nothing but a cowardly act.

What happens if this becomes the new normal?

Today it is my account. Today it is Telugu Scribe. Tomorrow, who will be next?

A government in a democracy should have the courage to face criticism...not silence those who question it.

Revanth Reddy government must answer.
@TeluguScribe 
@metaindia

India is the world’s largest democracy, where the right to peaceful assembly is guaranteed by our Constitution and safeguarded by robust institutions, an independent judiciary and a free media. As in every democracy, Indian citizens exercise this right subject to reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order. The authorities, for their part, act in accordance with the law, and our courts remain available to all for redressal of any grievances. 

The OHCHR’s concerns are therefore misplaced and constitute an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India.

In this context, OHCHR would also do well to devote comparable attention to large-scale protests elsewhere, consistent with its mandate of impartiality and non-selectivity.

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

Your bank account got frozen overnight. No notice, no call, no FIR against you. The bank just says “cyber cell instructions.”

This is happening to ordinary people across India every day. Here is what the law actually says, and what you should do. 🧵

🚨 Binance P2P se Bank Account Freeze? Poori Guide + Real Solution (2026)

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
• Bahut bade amounts ek baar mein mat trade karo
• Binance P2P risky hai India mein, agar ho sake toh avoid karo

Tag your friends jo P2P karte hain!

is the ECI compromised?  
 In March 2026, ahead of the Kerala Assembly elections (polling on 9 April 2026), a 2019 Election Commission of India (ECI) letter redistributed by the Kerala Chief Electoral Officer’s (CEO) office was found to carry the seal of the BJP’s Kerala unit. This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Later, a Deputy CEO and a Section Officer were relieved of election-related duties.livemint.comOpposition parties (CPI(M) and Congress) rejected the clerical-error account. They alleged compromised institutional neutrality, claiming seals were being “casually swapped” and questioning whether the ECI and BJP shared the same “power centre.” Some BJP responses labelled the circulation of the old document as misinformation or a political plot.thewire.inDeletion of posts controversyActing on an ECI directive (under the Model Code of Conduct), the Kerala Police cyber cell issued notices to X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, and numerous individual accounts. They demanded removal of posts sharing the letter that carried the BJP seal.  Police argued the content insulted the Election Commission, undermined its integrity and transparency, spread false claims about a rectified clerical error, and risked public order or communal harmony by potentially fuelling political division. Reports indicated hundreds of accounts were flagged (approximately 270 on X, 200 on Facebook, and 90 on Instagram). https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly condemns the imposition of this internet shutdown as it is not only disproportionate but also strikes at the heart of the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression, including the right to peacefully protest and to access information online, all recognized under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India.

(4/11)

Ordinary citizens are compelled to bear the incalculable cost in such situations, especially when internet shutdowns are accompanied by extensive road closures along and orders to close down metro stations across the city. This not only disrupts everyday transit for work, education, and access to essential services, but can also result in life-threatening consequences when access to emergency medical services and hospitals is also cut off or disrupted.

(10/11)

Since 2012, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has consistently documented the use of internet shutdowns in India through India's exclusive real-time Internet Shutdowns Tracker, available at https://t.co/q8n2oqVQhM. The suspension of mobile internet services during peaceful protests reflects the kind of opaque and disproportionate state action that constitutional safeguards as laid down in are meant to prevent. For further information about https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2's work on internet shutdowns and defending digital freedoms in India, please visit https://t.co/A8pDD7ylMx.

(11/11)

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon the the appropriate authorities, including the Government of NCT of Delhi and the Department of Telecommunications, Government of India to undertake the following measures:

1) Withdraw the order suspending mobile internet services in New Delhi immediately.

2) Publish the suspension order passed in relation to the shutdown of internet services on 09 October 2026 in accordance with the Supreme Court’s directions in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024. 

The suspension orders must provide:
(a) clear information on the following details, i.e., the authority issuing the order, date, time, and the specific area where the suspension will be in effect.
(b) clear reasons and supporting evidence demonstrating the necessity of the shutdown.

3) The order must be reviewed by the Review Committee within five (5) days as prescribed under Rule 5(3) of the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.

(8/11)

Internet shutdowns should not be used as a tool to curb peaceful protests. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 continues to observe a troubling trend where orders for internet shutdowns imposed in New Delhi are not published prior to its implementation. Non-disclosure of such orders raises serious concerns for freedom of speech and expression, access to information online and also for public transparency. Further, orders for internet shutdowns fail to provide substantive reasons, evidence of incidents of violence, and whether less restrictive measures were considered before implementing.

(9/11)

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Delhi ahead of the 10 October protest. The order remains unpublished, and the police communication conveying it is marked "Top Secret".

9 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the internet shutdown imposed in parts of Delhi ahead of the protest called for tomorrow, 10 October 2026, at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. A communication dated 9 October 2026 from the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Special Cell (HQ), Delhi to the nodal officers of Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Jio and MTNL, shared by the news agency ANI, records that the Union Home Secretary has authorised, on the request of the Delhi Police, the suspension of "mobile internet services (all technologies)" within a radius of four kilometres of the Janpath-Kartavya Path crossing, from 10 pm on 9 October to 10 pm on 10 October 2026. It refers to order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and is marked "Top Secret" at the top and bottom of the page.

As per a media report by Live Law, the Solicitor General informed the Supreme Court today that the shutdown is confined to "certain sensitive pockets" and will be reviewed on the basis of security inputs. The communication describes a circle of about 50 square kilometres across the centre of the capital, which takes in Jantar Mantar, Connaught Place, India Gate, Parliament, the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court, New Delhi Railway Station and hospitals including Ram Manohar Lohia and Lady Hardinge. This is about seven times the area of the suspension ordered around Jantar Mantar on 2 October, and it runs for twice as long.

Delhi Police has refused permission for the protest, and prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force in New Delhi district. Delhi Police asked for the gates of 57 metro stations to be closed from 9 pm today, and the Railways cancelled trains due at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin between 4 am and 2 pm tomorrow. Hearing a challenge to these measures today, the Supreme Court directed that there be no complete prohibition on metro and train services and asked the authorities to keep in mind the principle of proportionality. As reported, that order did not examine the internet shutdown. We call for the order to be withdrawn, and for mobile internet to remain available across Delhi tomorrow.

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public knows the area and hours of this shutdown from a police communication marked "Top Secret" that was shared by ANI, and not from the government. That communication records no reasons, and the order of the Union Home Secretary to which it refers has not been made public. This is now a pattern and the order for the shutdown of 2 October around Jantar Mantar became public four days later, when the Hindu obtained a copy.

This secrecy is contrary to the law declared by the Supreme Court. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Court held that "an order, particularly one that affects lives, liberty and property of people, must be made available". It directed the authorities to "publish all orders in force and any future orders" suspending telecom services, including the internet, "to enable the affected persons to challenge it before the High Court or appropriate forum". A democracy "sworn to transparency and accountability", the Court said, "necessarily mandates the production of orders as it is the right of an individual to know". The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, framed under Section 20 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, now provide that every suspension order "shall be published", must state its reasons, and must be limited to a clearly defined geographical area and a specified duration. No order may be made unless the authority has considered that its objectives cannot be achieved by any other reasonable means.

The communication shared by ANI invokes Rule 3 of these Rules, the same Rule that requires the order to be published. It is nevertheless marked "Top Secret", the highest security classification used by the Government of India. In January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued orders bearing the same number to suspend the internet at Singhu, Ghazipur and Tikri during the farmers' protest, and those orders remain available on the Ministry's own website. An order cannot be published and kept "Top Secret" at the same time.

The government has placed no evidence before the public that a shutdown makes a protest safer. The available research is to the contrary as a 2019 study of shutdowns and protest in India by Jan Rydzak, then at Stanford's Global Digital Policy Incubator, found shutdowns "much more strongly associated with increases in violent collective action than with non-violent mobilization". The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights reported in 2022 that many shutdowns justified on grounds of public safety or national security "were followed by spikes in violence" (A/HRC/50/55). In December 2021, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology recorded that neither the Department of Telecommunications nor the Ministry of Home Affairs had studied the impact of shutdowns.

A shutdown also prevents people from documenting and reporting what happens at a protest. The same UN report found that, “the inability to access tools to document and rapidly report abuses seems to contribute to further violence”. Without mobile internet, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A protester cannot upload a video as events unfold, and a person who is injured or detained cannot send a location to family or a lawyer. On 20 July 2026, mobile internet in Central Delhi was switched off amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters. In Manipur in 2023, video of an assault on two women on 4 May reached the public only on 19 July, while a shutdown imposed on 3 May was still in force. This is the impact an internet shutdown has which rather than preventing violence prevents the documentation of illegality.

Our demands:

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Delhi Police to:
1) Withdraw order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and keep mobile internet services running across Delhi on 10 October 2026.
2) Publish that order, and every other suspension order issued in connection with the protest, forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.
3) Withdraw the "Top Secret" marking, and stop classifying suspension orders and the communications that convey them to telecom operators.
4) Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and publish its final order, as the Supreme Court required on 23 February 2024.
5) Ensure that journalists and members of the public can record and report from the protest sites without obstruction.

On October 2nd, the government blocked BitChat in India without making the order public. We only found out through a notice on the iOS App Store.

BitChat uses Bluetooth mesh technology to pass messages from phone to phone. During Jantar Mantar 1.0, when the internet was shut and blocking vans jammed even SMS, protesters used it to find each other and share water and medicines.

Calling it a national security threat makes little sense. It only works over short distances, and the block only stops new downloads. Anyone can install it across the border and come back. The only people affected are citizens exercising their right to peaceful assembly.

What’s next, walkie-talkies and carrier pigeons? We’re filing RTIs and will keep pushing for transparency.

Statement: MeitY’s “enhanced diligence” advisory pressures platforms to police protest speech. It must be withdrawn.

October 9, 2026

On October 8, MeitY’s Cyber Laws Division sent an advisory to all social media intermediaries. It asks them to exercise “enhanced diligence” over false, misleading, manipulated or out-of-context content linked to “ongoing public events and developments”, to “identify, prevent and not promote” unlawful information, to label or “contextualise” misleading content, and to prioritise complaints from “authorised Government agencies” on public-order content. It takes effect immediately. MeitY has not published it and its text became public through MediaNama. It was issued as citizens protest in Delhi and Mumbai over the revision of electoral rolls, with a protest called at Jantar Mantar for October 10. We call on MEITY to withdraw it.

First, the advisory names no provision that empowers MeitY to issue it and such advisories are not issued under any law. Section 79(2)(c) of the IT Act conditions safe harbour on “due diligence” and on guidelines the Central Government may “prescribe”, that is, by rules notified and laid before Parliament under Section 87. The IT Rules recognise only “due diligence” under Rule 3 and “additional due diligence” for significant social media intermediaries under Rule 4. The phrase, “Enhanced diligence” used in this Advisory appears in neither. Further, MeitY’s proposed Rule 3(4) in the last round of Amendments mooted to the IT Rules, 2021, which has not been notified further confirms this does not have any legal character. Second, an advisory cannot alter the application of existing law. Rule 3(1)(b)(v) covers only misinformation communicated “knowingly and intentionally” that is “patently false and untrue or misleading in nature”. The advisory drops both qualifiers and adds “social tranquility”, neither that nor “misleading” is a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).

Third, facing an undefined standard platforms will censor more than the law requires. The advisory asks them to “identify, prevent and not promote” unlawful information and to “strengthen their existing monitoring”. This is proactive monitoring by another name, which the Rules contemplate only for narrow categories such as child sexual abuse material. Further, it is vague and does does not define “authorised Government agencies” or “priority”, and does not require platforms to tell users that a government complaint lay behind an action. Users will see only a platform decision. The State’s role disappears, and with it any route to challenge that role in court. The advisory governs public speech but is not itself public. It cites no statutory provision, is approved by an unnamed “competent authority”, and does not identify the events or content that prompted it.

We anticipate a huge spike in censorship over the next few days.

We call on MeitY to:
1. Publish the advisory in full, including any clause (v), and state the provision under which it was issued.
2. Withdraw it, or clarify that it creates no obligations beyond the IT Act and Rules and that “enhanced diligence” is not a condition of safe harbour.
3. Disclose which agencies are sending complaints under it, and how many.
4. Abandon the proposed Rule 3(4).

We also call on platforms to:
1. Disclose all government complaints and requests received under this advisory.
2. Act only on requests that meet the Shreya Singhal standard and Rule 3(1)(d).
3. Refrain from proactively filtering or downranking protest content on the basis of this advisory.
4. Notify affected users, including when an action follows a government complaint.

PS: We got the text of the advisory from @medianama' s website.
